report:
Your skepticism is well-founded — the claim as stated is false, or at least a significant overstatement.

**What's true:** In laboratory (in vitro) experiments, capsaicin has been shown to inhibit proliferation, induce apoptosis, and reduce migration in cultured breast cancer cell lines (e.g., MDA-MB-231), acting through pathways involving FBI-1 suppression and other signaling changes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/, https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT). Some animal-model work also shows effects on tumor growth and metastasis via capsaicin-sensitive sensory nerves.

**What's missing:** There is no clinical trial evidence that capsaicin treats or cures breast cancer in humans. A thorough review states: "The clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative," and that a "complete consensus... has not yet been reached" on whether capsaicin's net effect in cancer is protective or harmful (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). Fact-checkers reviewing viral claims explicitly note that lab studies don't translate to a "cure": researchers themselves cautioned that dietary or inhaled intake would be "insufficient," and practical delivery to tumor sites in the body is an unsolved problem (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).

**What does exist clinically:** Capsaicin patches are used, and studied in real trials (e.g., CAPTRANE, QUCIP), but for treating chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain in breast cancer patients — not for treating the cancer itself (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355).

**Conclusion:** Preclinical cell/animal studies suggest capsaicin has anticancer properties worth studying, but claiming it "treats breast cancer in humans" is unsupported and premature — no human trials show it cures or treats the disease. This is a classic case of overextending lab findings into a health claim.
